aspects.says: HashSet inherits an addAll that calls add for each element, so a subclass that counts in both add and addAll counts every batch twice.
basis: section:HashSet's addAll Calls add, So a Subclass That Counts in Both Counts Each Element Twice

aspects.says: Overriding fewer methods only moves the dependency: a subclass that counts only in add is right on HashSet and misses every batch on ArrayList, whose addAll never calls add.
basis: section:Counting Only in add Fixes HashSet and Breaks ArrayList: the Count Follows Code the Subclass Can't See

aspects.says: A class designed for extension offers a protected hook whose callers its javadoc names; LinkedHashMap's removeEldestEntry is called from put and putAll, while an override of put is skipped by putAll.
basis: section:Extend a Class Through the Hook It Documents: LinkedHashMap Calls removeEldestEntry from put and putAll

aspects.says: javac doesn't make a forwarding class implement equals and hashCode, and without them the wrapper's equality depends on which side is asked and hash lookups miss.
basis: section:javac Makes a Forwarding Class Implement Set's Methods, Not equals and hashCode

aspects.says: A forwarding wrapper counts each element once over any implementation, because the wrapped object's internal calls stay on the wrapped object.
basis: section:A Forwarding Wrapper Counts Each Element Once over Any Set, Because the Set's Own Calls Stay Inside It

aspects.says: A wrapper costs one forwarding line per interface method and is not an instance of the wrapped class, so a method declared to take that class won't accept it.
basis: section:A Forwarding Wrapper Counts Each Element Once over Any Set, Because the Set's Own Calls Stay Inside It
aspects.reason: a compile-time cost stated in one sentence; a graded run can't observe a call that doesn't compile
